item.title: “Monks, these three are inner stains, inner enemies, inner foes, inner murderers, inner adversaries. What three? Greed, monks, is an inner stain, inner enemy, inner…
item.description:
“Monks, these three are inner stains, inner enemies, inner foes, inner murderers, inner adversaries. What three? Greed, monks, is an inner stain, inner enemy, inner foe, inner murderer, inner adversary. Hatred, monks, is an inner stain … Delusion, monks, is an inner stain, inner enemy, inner foe, inner murderer, inner adversary. These, monks, are the three inner stains, inner enemies, inner foes, inner murderers, inner adversaries.”

From: Itivuttaka 88
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, the defilements of gold — because of which gold becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly workable — likewise,…
item.description:
“Monks, the defilements of gold — because of which gold becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly workable — likewise, monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. What five? Sensual desire, monks, is a defilement of the mind. Because of this defilement, the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. Ill-will … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … doubt are defilements of the mind. These, monks, are the five defilements of the mind. Because of these defilements, the mind becomes not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.33
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, then that monk, monks, should understand: ‘I have not fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘not falling away.’ … There are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … There are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, then that monk should understand: ‘I have not fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘not falling away.’ Thus, monks, is restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.98

item.title: Māra: You are young and beautiful, I am young and in my prime. With the five-tuned lute, Enjoy yourself, Khemā. Elder Nun Khemā: With this…
item.description:
Māra:

You are young and beautiful,
I am young and in my prime.
With the five-tuned lute,
Enjoy yourself, Khemā.

Elder Nun Khemā:

With this foul body,
Diseased and fragile —
I am disenchanted, disgusted.
Sensual desire has been uprooted.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears —
The aggregates are a chopping block.
What you call sensual pleasure —
I have now abandoned it.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed,
The mass of delusion is shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are defeated, Māra.

You worship the stars!
You worship fire in the deep forest —
You do not know the truth —
Fools think it is pure.

But I pay homage
To the Awakened One, the Supreme Man,
Who has escaped all suffering,
Following the Teacher’s instruction.

From: Therīgāthā 6.3
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Fear, suffering, and disease, A boil, and a dart, Bondage and mud, And also a womb — These are called sensual pleasures, Where worldlings become…
item.description:
Fear, suffering, and disease,
A boil, and a dart,
Bondage and mud,
And also a womb —
These are called sensual pleasures,
Where worldlings become attached,
Sinking into the beautiful,
They enter a womb again.
When a monk is ardent,
Not lax, mindful,
He crosses this dangerous path,
This path so hard to cross.
He sees beings living in fear,
Because of birth and aging,
Oppressed and conquered.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.56
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: The Blessed One replied to Bhadrāvudha: “Having expelled all desire for household things, Above, below, across, and in between — Whatever one clings to in…
item.description:
The Blessed One replied to Bhadrāvudha:
“Having expelled all desire for household things,
Above, below, across, and in between —
Whatever one clings to in the world,
By that very thing, Māra follows one.

Therefore, the wise one, knowing this,
Does not cling to anything in the world.
The mindful monk, seeing that beings
Are attached to what they cling to,
In Māra’s realm,
Should not long for any possession.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.13
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Therefore, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline. Monks,…
item.description:
“Therefore, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline. Monks, just as near a village or small town there is a large sala-tree forest overgrown with trumpet-flower creepers. Then a man comes who desires the welfare of that forest, its benefit, its security from bondage. He cuts down the crooked, weak branches, throws them out, and cleans the forest inside. He properly cares for the straight, well-grown sala saplings. Monks, after some time, that forest becomes grown, prosperous, and increased. So too, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 21 – Kakacūpamasutta

item.title: “Monk, ‘ant-hill’ is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent,…
item.description:
“Monk, ‘ant-hill’ is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to rubbing, pressing, breaking, disintegration, dissolution. ‘Smoking by day and blazing by night’—what belongs to daytime work, reflected upon at night—that is ‘smoking by night.’ What, after reflecting at night, is practiced during the day by body, speech, and mind—that is ‘blazing by day.’ ‘Brahmin’ is a synonym for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘Wise man’ is a synonym for a monk in higher training. ‘Sword’ is a synonym for noble wisdom. ‘Digging up’ is a synonym for arousing effort, striving. ‘Door-bolt’ is a synonym for ignorance; ‘lifting the door-bolt’ means abandoning that ignorance. ‘The wise man, taking the sword, dug up’ is the meaning.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 23 – Vammikasutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these four ignoble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging seeks what is subject to aging; being…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these four ignoble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging seeks what is subject to aging; being himself subject to sickness seeks what is subject to sickness; being himself subject to death seeks what is subject to death; being himself subject to defilement seeks what is subject to defilement. These, monks, are the four ignoble searches.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.255

item.title: “Monks, I will teach you about things that are bound and about binding. Listen. And what, monks, are the things that are bound? What is…
item.description:
“Monks, I will teach you about things that are bound and about binding. Listen. And what, monks, are the things that are bound? What is binding? Form, monks, is a thing that is bound. Desire and lust for form is the binding of form. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness, monks, is a thing that is bound. Desire and lust for consciousness is the binding of consciousness. These, monks, are called the things that are bound. This is the binding.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.120
